# Plumb — working agreement

## Protocols

**Before writing.** State which module owns the change, which
declared boundaries apply, and whether the change needs a new
external dependency.

**While writing.** Prefer the standard library to a new dependency,
and justify every dependency that survives that preference. Do not
create a module without declaring its boundary in the architecture.
Do not generalise before the third real use.

**After writing.** Run the gates. No completion claim without
command output.

# Architecture — Plumb

Modules and the dependencies they are permitted. An import that crosses a
boundary not declared here is a finding, not a style choice.

## crates/plumb-core

Responsibility: pure logic — parsing manifests, evaluating rules, rendering
Layer 1 artefacts. No network, no filesystem, no subprocess calls. This
boundary is load-bearing: anything that touches the outside world belongs in
`plumb-cli`, behind a trait so tests can stub it. Tests in this crate must
never contact the network.

May depend on: (none) — plumb-core has no internal dependencies.

## crates/plumb-cli

Responsibility: binary entry point — argument parsing, git invocation,
registry lookups, and the command implementations (`check`, `init`,
`adapters`, and future commands) that wire plumb-core's pure logic to the
outside world.

May depend on: plumb-core.

## docs/research/

Responsibility: the evidence base. `taxonomy.md` is the row-per-rule ledger
every enforced rule must trace back to (see .plumb/invariants.md, "the one
rule"); `sources.md` backs each row. Not code, and nothing in the crates imports it,
but every check the crates run and every rule in this working agreement
traces back to a row here.

May depend on: (none).

## docs/superpowers/

Responsibility: specs and implementation plans — the design record for how a
feature came to be, kept separate from the taxonomy so evidence and design
decisions do not get mixed together.

May depend on: (none).


# Conventions — Plumb

Frozen at bootstrap. A convention that lives in a head instead of a file
drifts between sessions; this file is the fix.

## File headers

Every Rust source file opens with, in this order:

```
// SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
// Copyright 2026 The Plumb Authors
```

## Error handling

No `unwrap()` or `expect()` outside test code. Errors propagate with
`anyhow::Result`. (`unwrap_or` and `unwrap_or_else` are different functions
and are fine anywhere.)

## Dependencies

Every third-party crate needs a row in
[docs/dependencies.md](docs/dependencies.md) saying why the standard
library is not enough. Plumb's own Tier A rule, applied to Plumb.

## Language

All code, comments, documentation and commit messages in English.

## Toolchain

Rust 1.97, edition 2024. `cargo` is not on the inherited bash PATH on this
machine — prefix invocations:

```bash
export PATH="/c/Users/Andre/.cargo/bin:$PATH"
```

```bash
cargo fmt --all
cargo clippy --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings
cargo test --workspace --locked
```

## Check versions before writing code

Check the current version and current API of a crate before writing code
against it. Do not write a version from memory. This is not pedantry: the
first implementation plan shipped an MSRV two years stale and a `ureq` error
match that no longer compiled, both because a version was recalled rather
than looked up. Dependencies track current releases, nothing is pinned by
hand, `Cargo.lock` is committed, and builds use `--locked`.

## Commits

One commit per step that changes files — a TDD cycle produces at least two,
the failing test and the implementation. Conventional Commits. Never amend,
never squash. Every commit message ends with:

```
Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
```


# Invariants — Plumb

Project-specific non-negotiables, one per heading, written as they emerge.
Empty is honest; aspirational is not.

## The one rule

Every rule Plumb enforces must trace back to a row in
[docs/research/taxonomy.md](docs/research/taxonomy.md). No source, no
rule. This applies to the maintainers, not only to contributors — a check
that seems sensible but has no row does not get added, because that is the
only thing separating this project from another opinionated linter.

Taxonomy §5 lists defects Plumb must *not* fight: function length,
cyclomatic complexity, readability thresholds. The evidence says AI already
matches or beats humans on those; do not reintroduce them.

## Tiers are evidence-graded, not severity-graded

| Tier | Enforcement | Evidence required |
|---|---|---|
| A | Blocks the build | Peer-reviewed, objective detection |
| B | Warns | Preprint, or thresholds needing calibration |
| C | Measures only | None — instrumentation for open hypotheses |
| Hygiene | Autofixed, excluded from defect counts | Style consistency, delegated to formatters |

Proposing a Tier A rule on a preprint is a rejection. Propose it as Tier B.

## Exit codes are a fixed contract

`0` clean, `1` a Tier A (blocking) violation, `2` warnings only. A run that
could not happen at all — not a repository, no git — exits outside that
contract, so a broken gate can never be read as a clean one.

## No test may contact the network

`plumb-core` has no network access by construction. `plumb-cli`'s registry
lookups are the only outbound calls Plumb makes, and the test suite never
exercises them against the real network — tests stub or fake the registry
boundary instead.
